Thirty-one years of missionary service ended with his death at Soochow, China, on July 16, 1922, when a launch on which he was traveling capsized, and he was drowned. His mortal remains lie buried in Chinkiang, his body lies, awaiting the Resurrection Day, and on the black granite tombstone, in English and Chinese is inscribed these words: "Greater love hath man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." WILL I. HUNT

Will I. Hunt was the second alumnus of the Savoy College to reach the signal honor of being a member of its collegiate department upon his completion of the A.B. course in 1887, and later it was to claim as one of its professors whose enthusiasm and energetic labors were enhancing the growing reputation of that institution during the middle 'eighties. His subsequent career shows that this association may have left its marks on the work of both the administration and the young teacher, for an observant residence has said that it was the influence of professors Halsel and Holland in inspiring young men and women to undertake ambitious endeavors and to serve for the student bed was to be observed in the achievements of the young faculty members of that period. If the College was in this manner to plant seeds of service in the hearts of young men—one in the ministry, one in missionary service, one in journalism, one in law, one in education, one in medicine—there may be traced the touch of the College and the character of its faculty members.

Back of Mr. Hunt were two generations of Baptist ministers. His father, W. S. Hunt, or M. Hunt, was fourteen years old when, in 1853, his family moved from Kentucky to Texas and settled in Savoy.
